To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we were able to show that ligand-induced changes in the conformational helices of a GPCR can be used to control the activity in an integrated enzyme.
the activity of an intracellular enzyme can be directly regulated by ligand binding in an engineered GPCR-enzymes fusion protein.
we have created a fusion protein of a GPCR (M3 muscarinic receptor) and an enzyme (firefly luciferase).
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new strategy to regulate enzyme activity by ligands.
the development of new tools for the control and manipulation of cellular functions.
the development of a new class of GPCR-enzyme fusion proteins that are directly controlled by ligand binding.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this work demonstrates that the M3 receptor can be used as a ligand-controlled switch for luciferase activity.
the M3 receptor-luciferase chimera represents a new tool to study ligand-induced conformatonal changes within GPCR.
the M3 receptor-luciferase chimera is a useful tool to monitor ligand-dependent conformational changes in the GPCR.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the third intracellular loops of GPCRs are suitable domains to control the activity by ligand-induced confectional changes.
ligand binding to GPCRs can be exploited for enzyme control.
the G protein-coupling machinery of GPCRs may be used to regulate the activity of intracellular enzymes by extracellular ligands.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ligand-induced confectional changes within the helix bundle can control enzyme activity.
the conformational changes of GPCRs can be exploited to control enzyme activity.
GPCR-enzyme fusions may be useful for controlling enzyme activity in living cells.
